taxista.desc_en: You're in Miraflores and want to take a taxi to Barranco. In Lima you agree on the price before you get in.

taxinuevo.desc_en: You're in a taxi in Miraflores. The driver is new and doesn't know the area well.

combi.desc_en: You take a bus to Barranco. The cobrador (conductor) shouts the stops. Then Augusto texts you.

cambio.desc_en: You change euros at an exchange office (casa de cambio) in Miraflores.

ex.w3-01: Good afternoon, sir. How much do you charge to Barranco?
ex.w3-02: I'm going to Barranco to see the sea.
ex.w3-04: It's very close. Will you do it for fifteen?
ex.w3-05: Love, I'm in Miraflores, in Kennedy Park.
ex.w3-06: Good evening. To Kennedy Park, please.
ex.w3-07: I don't have my card here, I'll pay you in cash.
ex.w3-08: Is the seafront far from here?
ex.w3-09: From Miraflores to Barranco is ten minutes.
ex.w3-11: It's too expensive, I'd rather order a taxi through an app.
ex.w3-12: How much is it from the airport to Rosario's house?

grammar.title: Ir a, en and de: to, in and from
explain: Where you're going: ir a. Voy a Barranco (I'm going to Barranco). Ir is irregular: voy, vas, va, vamos, van.
Where you are: en. Estoy en Miraflores. Where you're from or leave from: de. Soy de Holanda, de Miraflores a Barranco.
A + el becomes al, de + el becomes del: voy al parque, vengo del aeropuerto. With la it stays separate: voy a la playa.
grammar.compare: English: to, in, from. Spanish: a (to), en (in, at), de (from, of). Careful: 'I'm in Lima' is estoy en Lima, but 'I'm going to Lima' is voy a Lima, never 'voy en Lima'. And 'to the park' melts into one little word: al parque.

examples.en: From the airport to Kennedy Park.

8.goal_en: Take a taxi from Miraflores to Barranco and agree on a price of at most 15 soles beforehand.

9.title_en: Is there…, and how do I get there?

ex.w3-13: Excuse me, is there an ATM around here?
ex.w3-14: Sorry, madam, where is the bank?
ex.w3-15: Yes, there's a pharmacy on the corner.
ex.w3-16: Go straight on for two blocks.
ex.w3-17: At the traffic light, turn right.
ex.w3-19: The supermarket is two blocks away.
ex.w3-20: The ATM is next to the supermarket.
ex.w3-21: The church is opposite the park.
ex.w3-22: We're here. Stop at the corner, please.
ex.w3-23: It's here, thank you! How much is it?
ex.w3-24: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the seafront?

grammar.title: Hay or está, and understanding directions
explain: Hay means 'there is' or 'there are': you ask whether something exists. ¿Hay un cajero por aquí? There are two banks: hay dos bancos. Hay never changes.
Está is for something specific whose location you want: ¿dónde está el banco? El cajero está en la esquina. For several: están.
When someone gives you directions you'll hear commands in the usted form: siga (keep going), voltee (turn), pare (stop), cruce (cross). You can say them to the taxi driver too.
grammar.compare: English works the same way: 'there is an ATM' (any) versus 'the ATM is on the corner' (that one). Spanish: hay un cajero, el cajero está en la esquina. With 'a/an' you usually need hay, with 'the' you need está. 'Voltear' is Peruvian; in Spain they say 'girar'.

examples.en: Is there an ATM around here?

examples.es: El cajero está a dos cuadras.
examples.en: The ATM is two blocks away.

examples.es: Siga derecho y voltee a la izquierda.
examples.en: Go straight on and turn left.

exercises.why: The location of something specific (el banco): está.
Hay stays hay, also in the plural.

9.goal_en: Ask the driver if there's an ATM nearby, then guide him to the door: straight on, left or right, and 'pare aquí'.

ex.w3-25: Excuse me, does this bus go to Barranco?
ex.w3-26: I'm going to the municipal park. Where do I get off?
ex.w3-27: Sir, I'm getting off at the next stop, please!
ex.w3-28: How much is the fare to Barranco?
ex.w3-29: Every day I get on here, on Avenida Arequipa.
ex.w3-31: It's one o'clock, let's go and have lunch.
ex.w3-32: It's already half past three, how late!
ex.w3-33: See you at seven at the Puente de los Suspiros.
ex.w3-34: In Lima we live near the seafront.
ex.w3-35: Today I'm eating at Rosario's house.
ex.w3-36: Love, what time do you leave work?

grammar.title: Verbs in -er and -ir, and telling the time
explain: Verbs in -er and -ir work almost the same. Comer (to eat): como, comes, come, comemos, comen. Vivir (to live): vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, viven. Only 'we' differs: comemos, vivimos.
Careful: bajar (to get off) is an -ar verb (bajo, bajas, baja), subir (to get on) an -ir verb (subo, subes, sube).
What time? Es la una (one o'clock, singular). From two on: son las dos, son las tres. Halves and quarters: y media, y cuarto, menos cuarto. At seven: a las siete.
grammar.compare: Good news: Spanish counts the time like English. 'Half past three' is son las tres y media (three and a half), 'quarter to four' is las cuatro menos cuarto. Just remember 'es la una' (singular) but 'son las dos' (plural), and 'at seven' is 'a las siete'.

examples.es: Son las tres y media. Nos vemos a las siete.
examples.en: It's half past three. See you at seven.

exercises.why: Half past three = 3:30 = las tres y media.
One o'clock is singular: es la una.

10.goal_en: Ask the cobrador if the bus goes to Barranco and where to get off. Then agree on a fixed time with Augusto.

ex.w3-37: Excuse me, can I pay by card?
ex.w3-38: Good morning, what's the euro rate today?
ex.w3-39: I want to change a hundred euros into soles.
ex.w3-40: Could you give me twenty-sol notes, please?
ex.w3-42: Excuse me, the ATM isn't working.
ex.w3-43: I don't understand the number. Could you write it down for me?
ex.w3-44: Today the euro is at four soles ten.
ex.w3-45: Sorry, where can I change money around here?
ex.w3-46: Love, I can't get money from the ATM.
ex.w3-47: Do you charge a commission for changing euros?
ex.w3-48: For the bus I need a five-sol coin.

grammar.title: Poder: can, followed straight by the verb
explain: Poder means can or may. The o becomes ue, except for 'we': puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden.
After poder comes the whole verb (the infinitive) right away: ¿puedo pagar con tarjeta? No puedo sacar plata. Nothing goes in between.
In Peru people often say 'plata' for money (dinero). Sacar plata = to withdraw money.
grammar.compare: This one is easy from English: 'can I pay' = ¿puedo pagar?, with the verb straight after, just like in English. The difference is that the infinitive keeps its ending (pagar, cambiar, sacar) and 'poder' changes for each person: puedo, puedes, puede. And '¿me puede ayudar?' is as polite as 'could you help me?'.

exercises.why: After poder comes the infinitive: cambiar.

11.goal_en: Change 100 euros, repeat the exchange rate the clerk gives and ask whether you can pay by card.
